# Names that Scream {#sec-screaming}

Robert C. Martin coined the phrase *Screaming Architecture* [@martin2017clean] for the principle that a system's structure should announce what the system *does*, not how it is *implemented*. Open the codebase, read the top-level folder names, and the system should be obvious. Open a Division's source tree, read the slice folder names, and the capabilities should be obvious. Open one slice, read the file names, and that slice's responsibilities should be obvious.

The principle is simple. The discipline to follow it is not. Most codebases name by mechanism (*controllers*, *services*, *repositories*, *handlers*) because mechanism-naming is what frameworks teach. The result is architecture that mumbles. This chapter is about why business-intent naming is worth the discipline cost, what specifically to do and not do, and how to test whether a codebase passes.

## The principle

A name should answer: *what is this for?* The answer should be in the language of the business, not the language of the framework. A name that says *what is this implemented with?* fails. A name that says *what business outcome does this produce?* succeeds.

The Pizza Architecture of @sec-pizza makes screaming names *possible*. Without vertical slicing, screaming names have nowhere to live; a single capability is scattered across `controllers/`, `services/`, `repositories/`, with no folder representing the capability as a whole, and no place to put a screaming name. Vertical slicing gives each capability its own folder; naming gives the folder its voice.

The two doctrines reinforce each other. Pizza without screaming names produces folders called `slice1/`, `feature_a/`, *some-business-verb-here*/. Screaming names without Pizza produce folders named clearly but containing only one technical layer, with the other layers scattered. Both together: each capability has a folder; each folder has a name that announces the capability.

## Forbidden: technical suffixes

A suffix that describes the *mechanism* is a suffix that hides the *meaning*. The Codex bans the following from slice and module names:

| Banned suffix | What it actually means | Why it fails |
|---|---|---|
| `_handler` | "this handles something" | What does it handle? The suffix is content-free. |
| `_manager` | "this manages something" | God-modules in waiting. Avoid. |
| `_processor` | "this processes something" | Generic; describes nothing specific. |
| `_service` | "this is a service" | Tautological; the whole codebase is services. |
| `_helper` | "this helps with something" | The contents are whatever someone couldn't categorise. |
| `_util` | "miscellaneous" | The contents are whatever nobody bothered to think about. |
| `_impl` | "this is an implementation" | Of what? Where does the interface live? |
| `_worker` | "this does work" | Same problem as `_handler`. |

These suffixes survive in codebases because they let a developer save a name. "I don't know what to call this; I'll call it `UserHelper` and move on." The save is paid back continuously by every reader who has to open `UserHelper` to find out what it actually does. The accumulated reading cost dwarfs the original naming cost by orders of magnitude across the codebase's lifetime.

The discipline is to take the time, at the moment of naming, to write down the *thing the code does in business terms*. If you cannot, the code probably should not exist yet; its purpose is unclear and writing it will produce something whose role is also unclear.

::: {.callout-note}
## Counterclaim and response

**Counterclaim:** *Some technical concerns genuinely exist; there must be a NIF wrapper module somewhere, a JSON encoder somewhere, an HTTP-handler binding somewhere. Are those forbidden?*

**Response:** No. Technical concerns belong at the *boundary* of the system (the crust of the Pizza) and they may carry technical names because their job *is* technical. `reckon_db_crypto_nif` is fine; it is a Rust NIF wrapper and its name says exactly that. `loan_management_service` is not fine; it claims a business concern but hides behind a generic suffix. The rule is: business-concern modules carry business names; infrastructure-edge modules may carry technical names, but they live at the edge and do not pretend to be the centre.
:::

## Forbidden: CRUD verbs

The four-letter trap: *create*, *read*, *update*, *delete*. They look like verbs. They are not.

A *verb* describes an action with a business meaning. *Register* a user. *Renew* a loan. *Archive* a record. The verb tells the reader *what changed in the world*. *Create*, *update*, *delete* tell the reader *what changed in the database*. The two are not the same.

| CRUD (banned) | Business verb (use) | When |
|---|---|---|
| `create_user` | `register_user`, `enrol_member`, `onboard_customer` | Whichever describes what's actually happening |
| `update_user` | `amend_profile`, `correct_address`, `promote_to_admin` | Different verbs for different changes |
| `delete_user` | `archive_user`, `purge_user`, `suspend_user` | What is actually true after this |
| `update_loan` | `renew_loan`, `flag_overdue`, `record_return` | Loan operations have specific meanings |
| `delete_book` | `retire_book`, `withdraw_from_catalogue`, `mark_lost` | Books leave the system differently for different reasons |

The CRUD trap is especially dangerous in event-sourced systems because *events take their names from commands*. If the command is `update_loan`, the event becomes `loan_updated_v1`; past tense, suffix versioned, but devoid of meaning. A `loan_updated_v1` event tells a projection *something happened to a loan*; it does not tell the projection *which thing*. The projection has to inspect the event's payload to know whether to update the read-model row, change its category, or remove it entirely. CRUD events force projections to branch on payload content; business-verb events let them branch on event type.

The cure is to look harder. When you find yourself reaching for `update`, ask: *what is this update for?* If the answer is *the address was wrong, this corrects it*, then the verb is `correct_address` and the event is `address_corrected_v1`. If the answer is *the user got a promotion*, then the verb is `promote_user` and the event is `user_promoted_v1`. Different verbs for different reasons. The reasons matter; that is the point.

Some operations genuinely are generic; you might have a *amend_metadata* Desk that takes any metadata change and applies it. That's acceptable when the operation really is uniform. What's not acceptable is *using a generic verb to avoid thinking about specific verbs*. *Amend* is fine when amending is what's happening; *update* is never fine.

## Required: business verbs (commands) and past-tense participles (events)

The naming convention for slices and modules in CMD departments:

- **Commands**: `{verb_present}_{subject}_{version}`. Examples: `register_user_v1`, `issue_loan_v1`, `reserve_isbn_v1`, `flag_overdue_v1`, `retire_book_v1`.
- **Events**: `{subject}_{verb_past}_{version}`. Examples: `user_registered_v1`, `loan_issued_v1`, `isbn_reserved_v1`, `loan_flagged_overdue_v1`, `book_retired_v1`.
- **Slice folders**: same as the command, without the version. `register_user/`, `issue_loan/`, `reserve_isbn/`.

The pairing (command in present tense, event in past tense) is meaningful. The command represents *intent* (someone wants to register a user); the event represents *outcome* (the user was registered). Reading slip after slip in a Dossier, the past-tense participles tell a story: *user was registered, address was corrected, premium was activated, account was archived*. Each past-tense participle is a fact about what happened. The Dossier's stream becomes prose, almost.

QRY-side naming is similarly disciplined but uses different verbs:

- **QRY Desks**: `get_{subject}_by_{filter}` or `list_{subjects}_page` or `count_{subjects}_by_{filter}`. Examples: `get_loan_by_id/`, `list_overdue_loans_page/`, `count_active_memberships_by_branch/`.
- **Projections**: `{event}_to_{table}`. Examples: `loan_issued_to_loans.erl`, `book_retired_to_books.erl`.

Note the projection-naming convention is `{event}_to_{table}`; event-name on the left, target-table on the right. This makes the data flow legible at a glance: *the `loan_issued_v1` event flows into the `loans` table*. The convention is also greppable: `find . -name '*_to_*.erl'` enumerates every projection in the codebase. Tooling, not documentation, gives the global view of the read-side.

## The folder-walk test

The test for whether names scream: open the project, do not read any code, list the folders, and time how long it takes a person to understand what the system does. The benchmark is *ten minutes*. A new developer should be able to learn the major capabilities of a Division by reading its slice folders.

The library worked example, applied to this test:

```
apps/cmd_lending/src/
├── issue_loan/                                    ← intent obvious
├── renew_loan/                                    ← intent obvious
├── return_loan/                                   ← intent obvious
├── flag_overdue/                                  ← intent obvious
├── waive_late_fee/                                ← intent obvious
├── open_membership/                               ← intent obvious
├── suspend_membership/                            ← intent obvious
├── close_membership/                              ← intent obvious
├── on_book_registered_track_loanable/             ← integration point obvious
└── lending_aggregate.erl                          ← Dossier definition
```

Ten folders. Each folder name announces a capability. The integration point with the Catalogue Division is named so its source event (`book_registered`) and its action (`track_loanable`) are both visible. A new developer can read this list and know, in about thirty seconds: *Lending issues, renews, returns loans; tracks overdues with possible waivers; opens, suspends, closes memberships; reacts to Catalogue's book registrations*.

Compare what the same Division might look like with conventional naming:

```
apps/cmd_lending/src/
├── controllers/
│   ├── LoanController.java
│   └── MembershipController.java
├── services/
│   ├── LoanService.java
│   ├── MembershipService.java
│   └── IntegrationService.java
├── handlers/
│   ├── LoanEventHandler.java
│   └── MembershipEventHandler.java
├── repositories/
│   ├── LoanRepository.java
│   └── MembershipRepository.java
├── models/
│   ├── Loan.java
│   ├── Membership.java
│   ├── LoanStatus.java
│   └── MembershipStatus.java
└── utils/
    ├── DateUtils.java
    └── ValidationHelpers.java
```

Twelve folders and files. The reader learns: *this code has controllers, services, handlers, repositories, and models, and there is a `utils` for the rest*. It does *not* learn what the Division does. To learn that, the reader must open `LoanService.java` and read the public methods; only to find that the methods are `processLoan()`, `updateLoan()`, `handleLoanEvent()`, names that themselves are content-free. The reader descends through layers and never finds the screaming.

The folder-walk test is a useful interview screen for codebases. Open the top-level folder of any project, list the entries, ask a developer who has never seen the code what the system does. If they answer correctly in ten minutes, the names are screaming. If they cannot, the names are not.

## Where technical noise belongs

The Codex is not blind to the fact that real systems have technical concerns. Some code legitimately does technical work: encoding, parsing, networking, NIF wrapping, telemetry collection, retry middleware. None of this work is *business* work, and none of it should pretend to be.

Such code lives at the *boundary* of the system; the outermost ring of the Pizza, the crust. Its name can describe its mechanism because its job *is* mechanism. `reckon_gateway_grpc`, `reckon_db_hash_nif`, `evoq_telemetry`, `cowboy_handler_bindings`; these are infrastructure names, and their infrastructure-ness is honest. They sit at the wire, the file system, the JIT compiler. They are not slices of the Pizza; they are the plate the Pizza sits on.

The discipline is to keep this code *at the boundary*, named for what it is, and not let its naming style leak inward into the slices. The crust is allowed technical names; the cheese (the rings) and the toppings (the slices) are not. A slice called `reckon_db_loan_handler` is wrong; *loan* is a business concern; *reckon_db* and *handler* together drag the slice toward the crust where it does not belong. The slice is `issue_loan`. Whether it ultimately writes to reckon-db is an implementation detail and not part of the slice's identity.

## Anti-patterns in the wild

Three patterns appear repeatedly in codebases trying to be event-sourced but not committing:

### "Mixed-mode" naming

A codebase that names half its modules in business verbs and the other half in technical suffixes. The mixed mode is worse than fully technical naming, because the partial discipline lulls readers into thinking they understand a system they have not actually understood. A reader sees `register_user/` and thinks *the naming is good*; opens the next folder and sees `user_event_handler/`, and the inconsistency is more disorienting than uniformity. Pick a side. The Codex's side is business-verb.

### Generic lifecycle verbs

"Lifecycle" is a tempting abstraction. The temptation is to write code like:

```
start_phase, pause_phase, resume_phase, complete_phase
```

…and use it for every long-lived process. The result: every Dossier has the same four verbs; the verbs no longer mean anything specific; reading a Dossier's events tells you *something has phases* and nothing else. Resist this. Each long-lived process has its own verbs that describe its own work. A Planning Dossier (@sec-cycle) opens, shelves, resumes, concludes. A Rescue Dossier escalates, mitigates, resolves. A Loan Dossier is issued, renewed, returned. The verbs vary because the work varies; the verbs reveal the variation.

### Filename suffixes that duplicate the folder

A slice called `issue_loan/` with files inside it called `issue_loan_command.erl`, `issue_loan_event.erl`, `issue_loan_handler.erl`. The file suffixes duplicate the slice name and add the very technical suffixes (`_command`, `_event`, `_handler`) the discipline is trying to avoid. Better naming: `issue_loan_v1.erl` (the command), `loan_issued_v1.erl` (the event), `maybe_issue_loan.erl` (the handler; the `maybe_` prefix announces that this is a decision function that may say no). The files inside a slice carry the *role within the slice*; they do not duplicate the slice's purpose.

## What this enables

Names that scream are the second load-bearing claim of this book (the first being vertical slicing). Together they produce a codebase that *documents itself*. Onboarding takes hours instead of weeks. Code review is faster because the change is *in `flag_overdue/`*; the reviewer already knows what's being changed before reading a line. Refactoring is safer because moving code means moving it to its right-named folder, and the right-named folder is obvious.

The architectural commitments of Part I are now complete. Dossiers (@sec-dossiers) and Decisions (@sec-dossiers) provide consistency. The Pizza (@sec-pizza) provides structure. Pipelines and Process Managers (@sec-pipelines) provide coordination. The Reckon Cycle (@sec-cycle) provides the meta-process. Screaming names (this chapter) make all of it legible.

Part II walks the libraries that turn these commitments into running software. The first chapter of Part II covers *reckon-db* (the event store at the centre of every Pizza) and is the next door to open.
